flashcards.definition: Does a bridge's job for many more ports: each port is its own collision domain, and it sets up a point to point full-duplex link between any two nodes (microsegmentation).
A multiport repeater that works only at the Physical layer: every port receives what any other port sends, so all ports share one collision domain; it has no configuration options.
A Data Link layer device that splits a network into separate collision domains but keeps one broadcast domain, forwarding frames by MAC address; a switch does the same job for many more ports.
A shared media area in which only one node can communicate at a time; all hub ports are in the same one, a bridge creates separate ones, and each switch port is its own.
The single logical network whose nodes all process a frame sent to the all-1s MAC address (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff); a bridge keeps all of its segments in one.
The unique 48-bit hardware address of each Ethernet port, written in hexadecimal, that switches read from a frame's destination field to forward it.
A hot-swappable transceiver form factor for a single Gigabit Ethernet link.
A transceiver form factor that carries four 1 Gbps links, typically aggregated into one 4 Gbps channel.
The storage area network (SAN) protocol that some transceivers support in place of Ethernet; those transceivers are not compatible with Ethernet switches.

A transceiver, cable, or patch cord made for a different fiber type or wavelength than the rest of the link, such as a single mode transceiver on multimode fiber; it can cause significant signal loss.
How much light reaches the receiver at the far end of a fiber link, measured in dBm; losses from bends, aging, added splices, or extreme temperatures can leave it too weak.
The sum, in dB, of what the cable's attenuation, each connector, and each splice take from the light along a fiber path; it must be smaller than transmit power minus receiver sensitivity.
The fiber testing tool that, with an optical source, measures attenuation, the loss of signal strength from one end of a fiber cable to the other.
The port setting for the link's data rate (10, 100, or 1000 Mbps), normally auto-negotiated; when it is set by hand, both ends must match.
The port setting for full or half operation (hub ports run half; a switch sets up full links), normally auto-negotiated; when it is set by hand, both ends must match.
The default port setting that lets the two ends of a link work out speed and duplex between them; setting both ends to it generally fixes a mismatch caused by setting one end by hand.
The two ends of a link set to different data rates, usually by a manual setting; the link fails, and the port shows down/down.
One end of a link set to full and the other to half, so the link stays up but slows down, with high packet loss and late collisions.
Combining two or more cabled links into one logical channel for more bandwidth and redundancy; LACP can detect configuration errors and recover when one link fails.
The protocol that has bridges and switches organize themselves into a hierarchy under a root and block ports that would create loops, sharing its information in bridge protocol data units (BPDUs).
Frames that carry a data payload larger than the standard 1,500-byte MTU, so fewer frames are sent; every host, switch, and router on the path must support them and use the same MTU.
Choosing the switch with the lowest ID, made up of its priority value and MAC address, as the top of the spanning tree; an administrator should set the priority so a core switch wins.
The job spanning tree assigns each port: root port (forwards up toward the root), designated port (forwards down at the least cost), or non-designated (blocking) port, which would create a loop.
The five conditions a spanning tree port can be in: blocking, listening, learning (builds the MAC address table), forwarding, and disabled; only forwarding passes frames.
A redundant path, such as a patch cable joining two ports on one switch, that lets flooded frames circle without end; spanning tree should shut down the port to break it.

reference.title: Network Loop and Broadcast Storm Issues

flashcards.definition: The result of an unchecked loop: flooded traffic that pushes utilization near maximum and makes the switched segment unusable; spanning tree is meant to prevent it.

reference.title: Network Loop and Broadcast Storm Issues

flashcards.definition: Supplies electricity from a switch port over ordinary data cabling to a device such as a VoIP handset, IP camera, or wireless access point.
Connected devices needing more watts in total than a switch can supply across its ports, so some are not activated or reset intermittently; add a switch or use power injectors.

A powered device and switch port that cannot negotiate a compatible mode and power output, as can happen when a device that supports only the first version of PoE meets a port enabled for high-power PoE++ Type 4 devices.
The mode that delivers power over pairs 4/5 and 7/8, the pairs 10/100 Ethernet leaves spare; the other modes use pairs 1/2 and 3/6 or all four pairs.
A port shut off by the switch because of a fault, typically a spanning tree or port security violation, rather than by an administrator's command.
A port disabled on purpose with the shutdown command; the no shutdown command brings it back up.
A link aggregation group port whose channel has not been negotiated, so it shows up/down; both sides need matching settings, and with LACP at least one side must be active.
A checksum calculated from a frame's contents and sent as its frame check sequence (FCS); a receiver that calculates a different value rejects the frame, and rising errors usually mean interference.
Frames smaller than the 64-byte minimum, usually caused by collisions from a duplex mismatch or a legacy hub; otherwise, suspect a driver issue on the sending host.
Frames larger than the 1,518-byte maximum, usually from jumbo frames reaching a port not set to receive them, or 802.1Q framing on only one end of a trunk.
Incoming or outgoing frames an interface throws away, for reasons such as checksum errors, mismatched MTUs, frames too small or too large, high load, or permissions.
The switch command that lists the hardware addresses the switch has learned on each port, as stored in its CAM table.
The switch command that reports a port's line status (host on a good cable) and protocol status (Ethernet link established), plus its settings and its traffic and error counts.
The family of switch commands that display the switch's settings: the startup copy used at the next boot and the running copy, which can be compared to reveal an undocumented change.
The switch command that reports the PoE budget, the watts used and remaining, and what each port is supplying to its device.
